'''Thomas Brian Stowell''' {{post-nominals|list=[[Reih Bleeaney Vanannan|RBV]] [[Tynwald Honour|TH]]}} (6 September 1936{{snd}}18 January 2019), also known as '''Brian Mac Stoyll''',<ref>{{Cite web|title=Baase Brian Mac Stoyll – Death of Brian Stowell|url=http://celticcongressmannin.com/baase-brian-mac-stoyll-death-of-brian-stowell/|access-date=16 August 2020|website=Celtic Congress Mannin}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=5 December 2019|title=Shiaght Laa 5th December 2019|work=Manx Radio|url=https://www.manxradio.com/podcasts/shiaght-laa/episode/shiaght-laa-5th-december-2019/|access-date=16 August 2020}}</ref> was a [[Manx people|Manx]] radio personality, [[Celticist]], physicist, and author. He was formerly {{lang|gv|[[Yn Lhaihder]]}} ("The Reader") to the Parliament of the [[Isle of Man]], [[Tynwald]].<ref name="stowell">{{cite web|url=http://www.tynwald.org.im/links/tls/TC/Pages/C12.aspx#top|title=Chapter 12 - Clerk of Tynwald's Office|last=Phillips|first=Roger|work=Part b (ii) (Other Officers)|publisher=tynwald.org.im|accessdate=13 December 2012|location=Douglas, Isle of Man}}</ref> He is considered one of the primary people behind the [[Language revival|revival]] of the [[Manx language]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|date=27 January 2019|title='If it wasn't for Brian, the Manx language would have died out'|work=IOM Today|url=http://www.iomtoday.co.im/article.cfm?id=45317&headline=%27If%20it%20wasn%27t%20for%20Brian,%20the%20Manx%20language%20would%20have%20died%20out%27&sectionIs=news&searchyear=2019|access-date=5 August 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Whitehead|first=Sarah|date=2 April 2015|title=How the Manx language came back from the dead|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2015/apr/02/how-manx-language-came-back-from-dead-isle-of-man|access-date=14 August 2020}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite news|date=21 January 2019|title=Tributes paid to Manx Gaelic revival 'pioneer'|work=BBC|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-isle-of-man-46923558|access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref>

== Early years and the Manx language ==
Stowell was born in Douglas, Isle of Man on 6 September 1936<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iomtoday.co.im/manx-language/Dr-Brian-Stowell-receives-top.3669930.jp|title=Dr Brian Stowell receives top Manx cultural award|date=14 January 2008|access-date=25 July 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090703051619/http://www.iomtoday.co.im/manx-language/Dr-Brian-Stowell-receives-top.3669930.jp|archive-date=3 July 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref> to Caroline (''née'' Stothard) and Tommy Stowell.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last=Brian|first=Stowell|title=Gaelg as Fishig: Skeeal my Vea|publisher=Culture Vannin|year=2019|isbn=978-1-912668-03-8|location=Douglas|pages=12}}</ref> His mother's maternal grandparents were native Manx speakers, although they did not pass the language on to their children.<ref name=":2" /> He attended Murray's Road Junior School before attending [[St Ninian's High School, Douglas|Douglas High School for Boys]], where he excelled academically.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Stowell|first=Brian|title=Gaelg as Fishig: Skeeal my Vea|publisher=Culture Vannin|year=2019|isbn=978-1-912668-03-8|location=Douglas|pages=19}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Breesha|first1=Maddrell|last2=O’Meara|first2=Jamys|date=2019|title=Dr Brian Stowell RBV, TH (1936–2019)|journal=Folk Life|volume=57|issue=1 |pages=80–83|doi=10.1080/04308778.2019.1589024 |s2cid=182791972 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Stowell was inspired to start learning Manx after he read an article written by [[Doug Fargher]] passionately defending the Manx language in 1953.<ref name=":0">Stowell, Brian (May 2011). "[http://naaclt.org/resources/JCLL_2010-11_vol15-16_p169-184.pdf Manx Gaelic and Physics, a Personal Journey]" (PDF). ''Journal of Celtic Language Learning''. 15-16: 111–126.</ref> Stowell described himself as being "only dimly aware"<ref name=":0" /> before reading this article that there was a language other than English spoken on the Isle of Man. While still a student of Douglas High School for Boys he began attending lessons taught by [[Leslie Quirk]], who introduced Stowell to Fargher, and in turn to other members of [[Yn Çheshaght Ghailckagh]] such as [[Walter Clarke (linguist)|Walter Clarke]] and [[Bill Radcliffe]].<ref name=":0" /> During this period he accompanied Fargher and other members of Yn Çheshaght Ghailckagh as they recorded the remaining elderly native speakers. He spent his weekends, meeting in Fargher's office in Douglas and conversing only in Manx. After about nine months he became fluent.<ref name=":3" />

Although Stowell did have regular access to proficient speakers through Yn Çheshaght Ghailckagh, he found it difficult to access resources to learn the language, as well as hostile attitudes from non-Manx speaking members of the community:<blockquote>A deterrent at that time (and for a very long time after that) would have been the aggressive attitude of most other people: ‘What do you want to waste your time with that old nonsense for? That was never a real language!’ This was like some sort of fixed mantra.<ref name=":0" /></blockquote>Manx disappeared as a community language on most of the Isle of Man in the late 19th century.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Miller|first=Stephen|date=2007|title="Here the Manx language lingers, and may linger some time longer": Manx and English in Cregneash in 1901|journal=Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie|volume=55|pages=111|doi=10.1515/ZCPH.2007.108 |s2cid=162965158 }}</ref> It was a [[Prestige (sociolinguistics)|low prestige language]] and negative attitudes by much of the Island's population towards Manx posed significant difficulty for learners and established speakers alike:<ref name=":3" /><blockquote>"In the 1860s there were thousands of Manx people who couldn't speak English," says Stowell. "But barely a century later it was considered to be so backwards to speak the language that there were stories of Manx speakers getting stones thrown at them in the towns.<ref>{{Cite news|date=31 January 2013|title=Manx: Bringing a language back from the dead|work=BBC|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-21242667|access-date=6 September 2020}}</ref></blockquote>

== Life in Liverpool ==
In 1955 Stowell moved to [[Liverpool]] to study physics at the [[University of Liverpool]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Stowell|first=Brian|title=Gaelg as Fishig: Skeeal my Vea|publisher=Culture Vannin|year=2019|isbn=978-1-912668-03-8|location=Douglas|pages=44–45}}</ref> He met Pat Price, who became his first wife and mother to his two eldest children.<ref name=":0" /> After graduation Stowell worked as a physics teacher in a secondary school in Liverpool which he hated.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite interview|last=Stowell|first=Brian|interviewer=Adrian Cain|title=17. Working Life|url=https://www.learnmanx.com/media/brian%20pdf/17%20Working%20Life.pdf}}</ref>

He later worked at the [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]]. During this time, Stowell kept some of his sensitive research notes in Manx, knowing that he was the only person in the world who could understand them fully, often creating new scientific terms.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />

While living in Liverpool he attended [[Irish language]] classes arranged by [[Conradh na Gaeilge]],<ref>{{Cite interview|last=Stowell|first=Brian|interviewer=Adrian Cain|title=22. Learning Irish|url=https://www.learnmanx.com/media/brian%20pdf/22%20Learning%20Irish.pdf}}</ref> as he felt that they were "the next best thing to Manx."<ref name=":0" /> Stowell ultimately became fluent in Irish and taught classes in the language in Liverpool, although not without difficulty during [[the Troubles]]:<blockquote>And when the troubles came in [[Northern Ireland]] it was a bit difficult because people threatened the office in Liverpool about the class in Irish and it was….well they had to laugh in the end because I said, ‘Change the name to [[Celtic Studies]],’ and they did that and they made other threats because they thought that was the football club [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] in [[Glasgow]].<ref>{{Cite interview|last=Stowell|first=Brian|interviewer=Adrian Cain|title=24. Teaching Irish|url=https://www.learnmanx.com/media/brian%20pdf/24%20Teaching%20Irish.pdf}}</ref></blockquote> Stowell eventually used his experience learning and teaching Irish to translate the Irish language course ''[[Buntús Cainte]]'' into Manx, which became ''Bunneydys'' for the Manx language learning community''.''<ref name=":3" />

He gained a PhD in applied physics while lecturing at [[Liverpool John Moores University]] and became head of department.<ref name=":3" /> While lecturing in Liverpool, he taught Manx to [[Phil Gawne]] and Adrian Cain, who would both later hold the position of Manx Language Officer after Stowell was appointed in 1991.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite interview|last=Stowell|first=Brian|interviewer=Adrian Cain|title=27. Education Officer|url=https://www.learnmanx.com/media/brian%20pdf/27%20Education%20officer.pdf}}</ref>

In 1990, Stowell published ''Contoyrtyssyn Ealish ayns Çheer ny Yindyssyn'', his translation into Manx of ''[[Alice's Adventures in Wonderland]]''.{{fact|date=June 2025}}

Stowell's first marriage broke down in the mid-1970s and he married his second wife Julia Berney in 1982, with whom he had two girls.<ref name=":0" />

== Return to Mann ==
Stowell was appointed Manx Language Officer in 1991 and returned to the Isle of Man permanently with his family the same year.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Brian Stowell's autobiography|url=https://www.culturevannin.im/news/brian-stowells-autobiography-606861/|access-date=3 September 2020|website=Culture Vannin}}</ref><ref name=":5" />

The allocation of increased funding for the Manx language and the passing of the 2001 Education Act that allowed for the [[Manx language]], [[Manx literature|its literature]], and [[Manx history]] to be taught on the island's schools which in turn caused a drastic shift in attitudes towards the language:<blockquote>There has been a big change for you wouldn't, well I couldn't believe it, without doubt 50 years ago, 40 years ago, even 20 years ago, that a great change would come and for the most part that is on account of money from the Government. That's the main thing.<ref>Stowell, Brian. "[https://www.learnmanx.com/media/brian%20pdf/28%20Manx%20Today.pdf 28. Manx Today] y" (PDF) (Interview). Interviewed by Adrian Cain.</ref></blockquote>He made weekly broadcasts about history and current events on long-running, bilingual [[Manx Radio]] programme ''Moghrey Jedoonee'' for over 20 years.<ref>{{cite web|title=Reviving Manx - The Yale Globalist - An Undergraduate Magazine of International Affairs|url=http://tyglobalist.org/in-the-magazine/theme/reviving-manx/|accessdate=19 January 2019}}</ref>

In March 2006 Stowell's ''Dunveryssyn yn Tooder-Folley'' ("The Vampire Murders"), the first recorded full-length novel in Manx, was published despite the small numbers who could read fluently in Manx:<ref>[http://www.iomonline.co.im/ViewArticle2.aspx?SectionID=1143&ArticleID=1397570 ''Isle of Man Today'' article on ''Dunveryssyn yn Tooder-Folley''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060826083707/http://www.iomonline.co.im/ViewArticle2.aspx?SectionID=1143&ArticleID=1397570|date=26 August 2006}}</ref> <blockquote>The potential readership is very low indeed – only about 200 people can read it without much difficulty. You could rationalise why I went ahead by saying, “oh, it will be used for studying Manx.” But I never had that in mind at all. I just thought it'd be a great laugh to write a novel in Manx.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Cohen|first=Daniel|date=10 February 2012|title=First Person: Brian Stowel|work=Financial Times|url=https://www.ft.com/content/de38774e-5207-11e1-a30c-00144feabdc0|access-date=20 August 2020}}</ref></blockquote>Stowell died on 18 January 2019 after a period of ill health.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.manxradio.com/news/isle-of-man-news/loss-of-giant-of-manx-language-revival/|title=Loss of giant of Manx language revival|website=Manx Radio|accessdate=19 January 2019}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
In 2008, Stowell was awarded [[Culture Vannin]]'s ''[[Reih Bleeaney Vanannan]]'' ("Manannan's Choice of the Year") award for outstanding contributions to Manx culture. On [[Tynwald Day]] 2010, he was awarded the [[Tynwald Honour]], the highest honour that [[Tynwald]] can award a citizen.<ref>{{cite news|date=10 July 2010|title=Tynwald Day: Live video streaming|work=BBC News|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/local/isleofman/hi/people_and_places/newsid_8756000/8756534.stm}}</ref>

The {{Langx|gv|Aundyr Brian Stowell|links=|label=none}} ("The Brian Stowell Award") was created in memory of Stowell's achievements.<ref>{{Cite news|date=22 July 2019|title=New Manx creative prize in memory of Dr Brian Stowell|work=IOM Today|url=http://www.iomtoday.co.im/article.cfm?id=49748&headline=New%20Manx%20creative%20prize%20in%20memory%20of%20Dr%20Brian%20Stowell&sectionIs=news&searchyear=2019|access-date=14 August 2020}}</ref> It is awarded by the Manx language group, [[Pobble]], for any piece of creative work produced in Manx.<ref>{{Cite web|date=19 May 2020|title=Aundyr Brian Stowell 2019|url=https://pobble.im/News/Aundyr-Brian-Stowell-2019?|access-date=14 August 2020|website=Pobble}}</ref>

His autobiography {{Langx|gv|Gaelg as Fishig: Skeeal my Vea|links=|lit=|label=none}} ("Manx and Physics: The Story of my Life") was published posthumously in 2019.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news|date=3 December 2019|title=Manx language stalwart's posthumous autobiography|work=IOM Today|url=http://www.iomtoday.co.im/article.cfm?id=52502&headline=Manx%20language%20stalwart%27s%20posthumous%20autobiography&sectionIs=News&searchyear=2019|access-date=14 August 2020}}</ref>

==List of works==
* 1968: ''Gaelg Trooid Jallooghyn: Manx Through Pictures''
* 1973: ''Chronicle of The Kings of Mann and The Isles / Recortys Reeaghyn Vannin as ny hEllanyn'' with [[George Broderick]]
* 1974: ''Bunneydys: A Course in Spoken Manx'' (based on ''[[Buntús Cainte]]'')<ref name="Rebuilding">{{cite book |last= O'Néill|first= Diarmuid |title= Rebuilding the Celtic languages |year= 2005 |publisher= Y Lolfa |page= 403 |isbn= 978-0862437237 }}</ref>
* 1986: ''Abbyr Shen!''
* 1990: ''Contoyrtyssyn Ealish ayns Çheer ny Yindyssyn<ref>{{cite web|author=Everson, Michael|date=21 June 2010|title=Contoyrtyssyn Ealish ayns Çheer ny Yindyssyn - Alice's Adventures in Wonderland in Manx|url=https://www.evertype.com/books/alice-gv.html|access-date=20 January 2019|publisher=Evertype|language=gv, en}}</ref>''
* 1996: ''Bun-Choorse Gaelgagh''
* 1996: ''A Short History of the Manx Language''
* 1998: ''Y Coorse Mooar''
* 2005: ''Dunveryssyn yn Tooder-Folley'' (a serial story)
* 2006: ''Ealish ayns Çheer ny Yindyssyn''
* 2020: ''Gaelg as Fishig - Skeeal my Vea''
